title: The bow, the arrow, the target — om is the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the mark (2.2)
hook: the Mundaka turns meditation into archery: om is the bow, the self is the arrow, Brahman is the target
tomorrow: the two birds on one tree

segments.voice: Yesterday: from the blazing fire, sparks of the same form. Your line was sparks. Did you see someone who irritated you as a spark of the same fire? Day four hundred sixteen.

Watch an archer just before the release. The whole body goes still. The breath slows, then stops. The eyes stop darting. For one second, there's nothing in the world but the line from the arrowhead to the mark. Let the mind drift to dinner, and the arrow drifts with it. So when the Mundaka wants to describe meditation, it doesn't reach for a cushion or a mountain cave. It hands you a bow.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE THE RELEASE.` → `THINK OF DINNER, AND YOU MISS.` → `THE MUNDAKA HANDS YOU A BOW.`

segments.voice: Two verses do it. The first: take the great weapon of the Upanishad as your bow. Fit to it an arrow sharpened by meditation. Draw it back with a mind absorbed in that, and hit the target, dear one: the imperishable. Then the second verse spells out the picture. Pranavo dhanuh. Om is the bow. Sharo hy atma. The self is the arrow. Brahma tal lakshyam uchyate. Brahman is called the target. Then two instructions. It must be struck by one who isn't careless, apramatta, undistracted. And then: sharavat tanmayo bhavet. Like the arrow, become one with it. Look at what happens when an arrow hits its mark. It doesn't stay separate, hovering an inch away. It goes in. It becomes part of the target. Tanmaya means made of that, full of that, absorbed in it. You met that -maya, made of, a few weeks ago in the Taittiriya: the self made of food, of breath, of mind. Now the text asks you to become tan-maya, made of that. Why is om the bow? Teachers explain that the sound, chanted or held in the mind, gathers attention and sends it. The next verse adds: know the one self alone, in which sky and earth and mind are woven. Let go of other talk. This is the bridge to the deathless. And then a blessing: may you cross safely to the far shore, beyond darkness.
screen: `THE UPANISHAD IS THE BOW.` · `OM THE BOW, THE SELF THE ARROW.` · `BRAHMAN THE TARGET.` · `LIKE THE ARROW, BECOME ONE WITH IT.` · then, large: `TANMAYA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of archery. Sit tall, like a drawn bow. If you'd like, let a soft om come out on the breath, or simply hear it inside. Let that sound gather your attention, the way a bow gathers its pull. Then let the attention fly to one point: the stillness after the sound. When the mind wanders, and it will, notice it, without blame, and draw the bow again. Undistracted, for one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
The bow. In the Mundaka, om is the bow, the self is the arrow, Brahman is the target, and the archer becomes one with it, like the arrow in the mark.
Your line: tanmaya, become one with it. Today, choose one task and give it the archer's attention, all of you, until you're made of it. Day four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Hindus who meditate with om chant it aloud or hold it in the mind, and some teachers use the Mundaka's bow and arrow to describe how the sound gathers attention toward one point.

match.prompt: the archer's picture — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: the arrow hits the mark. in the Mundaka's picture, what's the archer told to do?

fork.reveal: sharavat tanmayo bhavet: like the arrow, become one with it. the arrow doesn't hover beside the mark; it goes in.

original.note: Sanskrit tanmaya: tat, that, + maya, made of. 'like the arrow, become one with it', Mundaka 2.2.4.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means emptying your mind.
what it means: in the Mundaka, meditation is archery: om sends the self toward Brahman, undistracted, until it becomes one with it.
what a scholar hears: praṇavo dhanuḥ śaro hy ātmā brahma tal lakṣyam ucyate; apramattena veddhavyaṃ śaravat tanmayo bhavet (2.2.4).

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 2.2.3, 2.2.5–2.2.6 (the great weapon; the bridge to the deathless; crossing beyond darkness)

notes: 2.2.3–2.2.6 paraphrased from memory, including the blessing 'svasti vah paraya tamasah parastat' (2.2.6). Confirm.
Spoken transliterations (pranavo dhanuh; sharo hy atma; brahma tal lakshyam ucyate) simplified; Confirm.
'Archery was a noble art; the epics are full of bowmen' is a general remark (Arjuna, Rama, Karna).
